text: Disruption of cell adhesion drives cancer dedifferentiation, invasion, and metastasis. Desmosomes and hemidesmosomes mediate cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesion. Immunohistochemistry of desmoglein 1 (DSG1), DSG2, DSG3, desmocollin 2 (DSC2), integrin beta 4 (ITGB4), laminin gamma chain 2 (LAMC2), and collagen type 17 alpha 1 (COL17A1) was performed in 51 oral squamous cell carcinoma cases. In normal oral epithelium, DSG1, DSG3, DSC2, and COL17A1 localized to the plasma membrane; ITGB4 and mature LAMC2 to the basement membrane. In cancer, DSG1, DSG3, DSC2, and COL17A1 decreased and internalized cytoplasmically; DSG2, ITGB4, and LAMC2 showed induced cytoplasmic expression in stroma-facing cells. Reduced DSG3 and DSC2 correlated with less differentiation, greater invasiveness, and higher nodal metastasis; lower COL17A1 and higher LAMC2 also indicated aggressive phenotype. Aberrant expression and altered localization of desmosomal and hemidesmosomal proteins thus associate with aggressive clinicopathological features, supporting that disturbed keratin-associated anchoring junctions confer aggressive cancer features.
